cards.title: The capacity region of the general two-way channel
cards.formal: Determine the capacity region C(W) for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless two-way channel W with independent messages and causal adaptive encoders as defined below. The intended form or evaluability of a new characterization remains unspecified; unrestricted multiletter characterizations are already known.
cards.why: Determines the fundamental value of interaction in simultaneous bidirectional communication.

cards.definitions: Fix nonempty finite input sets X₁,X₂ and output sets Y₁,Y₂, and numbers W(y₁,y₂|x₁,x₂)≥0 summing to 1 over the output pair for each input pair. A length-n code has positive integer message counts M₁,M₂ and independent uniform messages U_i∈{1,…,M_i}. At time t=1,…,n, terminal i transmits X_i,t=f_i,t(U_i,Y_i,1,…,Y_i,t−1), where f_i,t is deterministic. Given both messages and the entire preceding history, the output pair at time t is sampled according to W at the current input pair. Both inputs are selected before either current output is observed. Terminal i uses a deterministic decoder g_i(U_i,Y_i^n) to estimate U_(3−i). Average joint error is the probability that at least one estimate is wrong, over the messages and channel outputs. A nonnegative rate pair (R₁,R₂) is achievable if codes with block lengths tending to infinity have joint error tending to zero and liminf (log₂ M_i)/n≥R_i for both i. C(W) is the closure of these achievable pairs in R². R₁ measures communication from terminal 1 to 2, and R₂ from 2 to 1, in bits per channel use. Codes and W are known in advance. There are no other communication links or shared random seeds. Local computation is unrestricted.
cards.answer_criterion: A capacity theorem must establish both achievability and a matching converse for every W in the stated model. A completed benchmark must additionally specify the representation or evaluability required of the answer, distinguishing it from a known multiletter characterization. Replacing the adaptive encoders by encoders that ignore past outputs changes the problem.

context_blocks.title: A conversation through one channel
context_blocks.text: Each terminal wants to send its own message and decode the other terminal’s message. What it transmits next may depend on what it has heard so far. The channel law has no memory, but the resulting conversation generally does: the encoding rules retain past observations. The two-dimensional region records the achievable tradeoff between the two directions.

context_blocks.title: Knowing your own signal can remove ambiguity
context_blocks.text: For binary inputs and outputs Y₁=Y₂=X₁ XOR X₂, each terminal knows the bit it sent and can recover the other bit. Both directions can therefore operate at one bit per use. For the binary multiplying channel Y₁=Y₂=X₁X₂, transmitting zero always produces zero, so that terminal learns nothing about the other current input. The two examples have identical alphabet sizes but different information tradeoffs.

context_blocks.title: Adaptation is part of the target
context_blocks.text: Shannon’s classical inner bound uses inputs that do not adapt to received symbols. It need not equal the general adaptive capacity region. Some channel families have exact capacity results with no benefit from adaptation; these are special cases. Willems’s July 2026 lecture discusses the general unresolved question and the separation between known bounds, including the binary multiplying channel.

context_blocks.title: What a new characterization must add
context_blocks.text: Known multiletter formulas already express capacity using arbitrarily long blocks. Cheng and Devroye explicitly distinguish these from a single-letter expression with bounded auxiliary alphabets. Such an expression and a terminating numerical approximation algorithm are distinct answer requirements. The original card does not specify either precisely, so this review retains an explicit formulation gap instead of claiming that the operational definition settles the problem.

sentences: Two terminals exchange independent messages through the same channel.
Each can adapt its next transmission to the outputs it has already received.
The capacity region records pairs of rates attainable with vanishing average decoding error.
Known bounds and exact special cases do not settle the general adaptive problem.
The source still needs to state what form of new characterization is required beyond known multiletter formulas.

cards.context:
Each terminal wants to send its own message and decode the other terminal’s message. What it transmits next may depend on what it has heard so far. The channel law has no memory, but the resulting conversation generally does: the encoding rules retain past observations. The two-dimensional region records the achievable tradeoff between the two directions.

For binary inputs and outputs Y₁=Y₂=X₁ XOR X₂, each terminal knows the bit it sent and can recover the other bit. Both directions can therefore operate at one bit per use. For the binary multiplying channel Y₁=Y₂=X₁X₂, transmitting zero always produces zero, so that terminal learns nothing about the other current input. The two examples have identical alphabet sizes but different information tradeoffs.

Shannon’s classical inner bound uses inputs that do not adapt to received symbols. It need not equal the general adaptive capacity region. Some channel families have exact capacity results with no benefit from adaptation; these are special cases. Willems’s July 2026 lecture discusses the general unresolved question and the separation between known bounds, including the binary multiplying channel.

Known multiletter formulas already express capacity using arbitrarily long blocks. Cheng and Devroye explicitly distinguish these from a single-letter expression with bounded auxiliary alphabets. Such an expression and a terminating numerical approximation algorithm are distinct answer requirements. The original card does not specify either precisely, so this review retains an explicit formulation gap instead of claiming that the operational definition settles the problem.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
